title: Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law Amendment Bill 2014
short_title: Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law Amendment Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would amend national domestic commercial vessel safety law to give the regulator more discretion over certificates and clarify administrative and review arrangements.
The Australian Maritime Safety Authority would gain explicit vessel survey functions, while state and Northern Territory delegates could pass powers to additional agency staff.
The amendments would commence on Royal Assent and align vessel definitions with other marine safety legislation, alongside corrections to provisions governing reviewable decisions.
changes: The regulator could choose whether to vary, suspend or revoke survey and operation certificates in specified circumstances.
A government vessel definition would be added using the meaning in the Navigation Act.
Specified decisions by marine safety inspectors would be expressly identified as reviewable.
Marine safety inspectors making reviewable decisions would have to notify the person concerned.
Regulations could govern how vessel surveys are conducted.
summary.affected: Domestic commercial vessel operators, certificate holders, accredited surveyors, marine safety inspectors and Commonwealth, state and Northern Territory regulators would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Warren Truss
speeches.brief: Introduced amendments to the Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law Act 2012, agreed by all state and territory transport ministers, to give the national regulator more discretion over vessel certificate suspensions and align the definition of 'defence vessel' with the Navigation Act 2012.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Said the Greens would not block the Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law Amendment Bill 2014 from passing the House, but flagged concerns about section 11's delegation of authority and its effect on appeal rights, to be examined further as the bill proceeds to the Senate.
